children: Vertical Aerospace (ETVL) is exploring strategic and financial partnerships as the electric-aircraft developer looks for ways to fund the next stage of its eVTOL program.

The British company said Thursday it has begun a review of strategic alternatives and retained Jefferies as financial adviser. Vertical didn’t set a timetable for the process and cautioned that the review may not result in a transaction or other strategic change.
The move comes as Vertical
shifts its focus from demonstrating its aircraft technology toward the considerably more capital-intensive tasks of certification, industrialization and eventual commercial production.

For investors, the strategic review puts financing squarely in focus. Vertical recently raised about $100 million, giving it additional resources to continue development, but bringing an aircraft through certification and into volume production can require substantial additional capital. A strategic partner could provide funding as well as manufacturing, supply-chain or commercial expertise, while other alternatives could potentially include additional equity investment or a broader corporate transaction.
From flight testing to financing
Vertical

said 2026 marked significant progress for its aircraft program. The company became the second developer globally to complete a piloted transition flight in a full-scale tiltrotor eVTOL, according to the announcement.
The aircraft subsequently performed five consecutive days of piloted transition demonstrations at the Farnborough International Airshow.

CEO Stuart Simpson said Vertical believes the technology has been substantially de-risked and that the company is now entering a different stage of its development. With attention turning toward certification, manufacturing and commercialization, management believes this is an appropriate point to examine financing and partnership options.
Vertical also recently named former Airbus Commercial Aircraft CEO Fabrice Brégier chairman, adding an aerospace industry veteran as the company prepares for that transition.
Key milestones remain on track
Vertical
said the strategic review won’t interrupt its operations, certification work or existing commercial commitments.

The company continues to target completion of its Critical Design Review by the end of 2026. Its initial aircraft production facility and an expanded Energy Centre also remain scheduled to open later this year.
Those milestones will be important for investors watching whether Vertical can convert successful flight demonstrations into a certifiable and commercially manufacturable aircraft.

Vertical is developing Valo, a piloted four-passenger electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, along with a hybrid-electric version intended to provide greater range and flexibility. The company lists Honeywell Aerospace, Syensqo and Sonaca among its aerospace partners.

Vertical says it has about 1,500 pre-orders across four continents, including commitments involving American Airlines, Avolon, Bristow, GOL and Japan Airlines. Some customer obligations are expected to be fulfilled through third-party agreements.

The strategic review now adds another potential catalyst, as well as another source of uncertainty, for shareholders. Vertical said it won’t provide updates unless its board approves a specific course of action or determines that further disclosure is appropriate.
